task_3.title: Speed up instantiation of frozen slotted attrs classes
task_3.description: Upgrading from attrs 21.4.0 to 22.1.0 improves the runtime cost of creating frozen slotted classes while preserving their initialization semantics. Construction should still populate fields, apply converters, and keep instances frozen after initialization, but with lower overhead during object creation.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to attrs 22.1.0 makes frozen slotted attrs classes faster to instantiate without changing their observable initialization behavior, conversion behavior, hash-cache setup, or frozen semantics after construction.

expectation.grounded: For attrs classes created with both frozen and slots enabled, generated initialization should continue to assign constructor-provided values, including converted values, by bypassing normal setattr interception through object.__setattr__ semantics. Any cached hash state initialized during construction should follow the same bypassed assignment path. After initialization completes, the class must still behave as frozen and no public API changes should be required from users.
expectation.conceptual: Creating frozen slotted attrs instances should become faster in the new version, while the objects produced by construction should look and behave the same as before. Field values should still be populated correctly, conversions should still occur, and the resulting instances should remain immutable after they are created.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the public constructor contract for frozen slotted attrs classes. Initialization must still succeed for normal fields, converter-backed fields, and cached-hash scenarios, and the class must remain frozen after construction. The upgrade must not introduce a requirement for callers to change how they declare or instantiate these classes.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade is a performance optimization, not a behavioral redesign. Existing application code using frozen slotted attrs classes should keep working the same way, aside from seeing lower object-creation overhead.

behavior: Instantiation of attrs classes that are both frozen and slotted should have lower runtime overhead than in 21.4.0.
During construction of a frozen slotted attrs class, field assignment should still bypass frozen setattr restrictions so initialization can populate instance state successfully.
Converter-backed attributes on frozen slotted attrs classes should still be converted before their final stored value is assigned during initialization.
If cached hash support is enabled for a frozen slotted attrs class, construction should still initialize the internal hash-related state without changing post-construction frozen behavior.
After initialization, frozen slotted attrs instances should still reject ordinary attribute mutation just as before the upgrade.
acceptance_criteria: When an application upgrades from attrs 21.4.0 to 22.1.0 and instantiates a frozen slotted attrs class, it should create an equivalent initialized object without requiring code changes.
When a frozen slotted attrs class defines converters, constructing an instance should still store converted field values in the resulting object.
When a frozen slotted attrs class uses cached hash behavior, constructing an instance should still leave the object in a valid state for later hash use.
When construction of a frozen slotted attrs instance has completed, attempting to mutate its attributes through normal assignment should still be blocked by frozen semantics.
When comparing runtime behavior before and after the upgrade, creating frozen slotted attrs instances should be faster in 22.1.0 while preserving the same externally visible construction results.

task_2.title: Remove reliance on attrs.Attribute.cmp
task_2.description: The upgrade removes the deprecated `cmp` attribute from `attrs.Attribute` instances. Consumers must use the supported `eq` and `order` metadata instead, while the `cmp` argument on `attr.s` and `define` remains available as a shortcut for configuring equality and ordering together.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure applications upgrading to 22.1.0 no longer depend on `attrs.Attribute.cmp` and continue to observe the intended comparison behavior through the supported `eq` and `order` APIs and the retained `cmp` shortcut on class definition helpers.

expectation.grounded: `attrs.Attribute` objects returned by field introspection must no longer expose the deprecated `.cmp` attribute. Consumers should read comparison configuration from `.eq` and `.order` instead. The `cmp` argument on `attr.s` and `define` remains supported and continues to act as a shortcut for setting equality and ordering together.
expectation.conceptual: After upgrading, the deprecated field-introspection shortcut for combined comparison state is gone, but supported comparison configuration still works. Code should rely on the explicit equality and ordering settings, while class definitions may continue using the comparison shortcut that configures both behaviors together.

constraints.grounded: Do not require or restore `attrs.Attribute.cmp`. Preserve the observable meaning of `eq` and `order` on `attrs.Attribute`, and do not change the runtime behavior of the `cmp` argument on `attr.s` or `define`.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should remove only the deprecated introspection surface and must not alter how comparison support is configured or observed through the supported APIs.

behavior: `attrs.Attribute` no longer provides a `.cmp` member at runtime.
Comparison metadata on introspected fields is represented through the existing `.eq` and `.order` members.
Using the `cmp` argument on `attr.s` or `define` continues to configure equality and ordering together rather than being removed by this upgrade.
acceptance_criteria: When code introspects fields and obtains an `attrs.Attribute`, it should not expect a `.cmp` attribute to be available.
When code needs to determine comparison behavior from an `attrs.Attribute`, it should be able to do so from the supported `eq` and `order` values.
When a class is declared with the `cmp` argument on `attr.s` or `define`, the resulting class should continue to derive equality and ordering behavior from that shortcut after the upgrade.

task_5.title: Add minimum-length validation for attrs fields
task_5.description: Version 22.1.0 adds a public minimum-length validator for attrs fields. Users can now enforce that strings and other sized values meet a lower length bound during attribute validation, with too-short values rejected through normal runtime validation.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading to attrs 22.1.0 can declare a minimum allowed length for field values using the library's built-in validator API, and that too-short strings or other sized iterables are rejected during attribute validation.

expectation.grounded: Provide a public `min_len(length)` validator in the attrs validators API. When attached to an attribute, it must allow values whose `len(value)` is greater than or equal to the configured minimum and raise `ValueError` when `len(value)` is smaller than that minimum. The validator must be part of the exported built-in validators surface.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to configure a built-in minimum-length check on attrs-managed fields. Values meeting the threshold should be accepted, and values below the threshold should fail validation with a value error.

constraints.grounded: The validator must enforce only a lower bound on length, treat the configured minimum as inclusive, and behave consistently for value types that expose `len()`. Existing maximum-length validation behavior and other validators must remain unaffected.
constraints.conceptual: The change should add minimum-length enforcement without changing unrelated validation semantics. It should work consistently for sized values and accept values exactly at the configured minimum.

behavior: `min_len(length)` is available as a built-in attrs validator.
A field using `min_len(length)` accepts values whose length is equal to or greater than the configured minimum.
A field using `min_len(length)` raises `ValueError` when given a value whose length is below the configured minimum.
The validator applies to strings and other sized iterable or container values that define a length.
acceptance_criteria: When an attrs field is configured with `min_len(2)` and initialized with a string of length 2 or more, it should be accepted.
When an attrs field is configured with `min_len(2)` and initialized with another sized value whose length is 2 or more, it should be accepted.
When an attrs field is configured with `min_len(2)` and initialized with a sized value whose length is less than 2, it should raise `ValueError`.
When importing built-in validators from the public attrs validators API, `min_len` should be available.

task_4.title: Honor custom equality keys in generated hashes
task_4.description: The upgrade fixes generated hashing for attrs classes so that attributes with a custom equality key are transformed the same way for hashing as they are for equality. This brings hash behavior in line with documented equality semantics and prevents mismatches where equal objects could previously produce different hashes or fail to hash based on the raw attribute value.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that generated hashes for attrs-based classes stay consistent with custom attribute equality keys, so objects that are considered equal through an `eq` key also hash according to that same normalized value.

expectation.grounded: For classes using attrs-generated `__hash__`, any attribute declared with a custom `eq` key callable, such as via `attr.ib(eq=callable)`, must contribute to the hash using the callable's result rather than the raw stored value. This should align generated hashing with generated equality for the same attribute and allow hashing to depend on the normalized comparison key when that key is hashable.
expectation.conceptual: If an attribute uses custom normalization for equality, hashing should use that same normalized representation. Objects that compare equal because of that normalization should also produce matching hash values.

constraints.grounded: The behavioral change should be limited to attributes that define a custom `eq` key. Attributes without a custom equality key must continue to hash from their original value, and the fix must not require callers to change how they declare or instantiate attrs classes.
constraints.conceptual: Only normalized-equality fields should change hash behavior. Existing hash behavior for ordinary fields should remain stable, and the feature should work through the existing public attrs API.

behavior: Generated `__hash__` now applies an attribute's custom `eq` key callable before hashing that attribute's contribution.
Instances whose differing raw values collapse to the same equality key now produce the same hash when their other hashed fields are equal.
Hash generation can succeed for values that are not directly hashable when the configured equality key produces a hashable comparison value.
Attributes without a custom equality key continue to contribute their raw value to generated hashes.
acceptance_criteria: When an attrs class generates `__hash__` and an attribute has a custom `eq` key, hashing an instance should be based on the transformed comparison key for that attribute rather than the raw stored value.
When two instances differ only in raw values that normalize to the same equality key for a hashed attribute, they should produce the same hash.
When a hashed attribute has no custom equality key, differing raw values should continue to produce different hash contributions under normal hashing rules.
When a raw attribute value is not directly hashable but its custom equality key returns a hashable value, hashing the instance should succeed using the normalized key.

task_1.title: attrs 22.1.0 Python-3-only upgrade
task_1.description: attrs 22.1.0 drops Python 2.7 support and standardizes the package on supported Python 3 runtimes. The upgrade also makes a small set of user-visible API semantics more explicitly Python-3-native, including immutable copied attribute metadata, support for composing multiple deep iterable member validators, and more consistent annotation exposure for converter wrappers and generated initializers.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to attrs 22.1.0 removes Python 2.7 compatibility assumptions and preserves correct Python-3-native behavior for attrs decorators, validators, converters, and attribute metadata.

expectation.grounded: attrs 22.1.0 must be treated as a Python >=3.5 dependency; Python 2.7 is no longer a supported runtime. On supported interpreters, attrs-generated `__init__` methods should expose native keyword-only parameters, `validators.deep_iterable()` should accept either a single member validator or a list or tuple of validators and compose them, `Attribute.metadata` should be exposed as a read-only mapping proxy backed by a shallow copy of the supplied mapping, and converter wrappers such as `converters.optional()` and `converters.pipe()` plus attrs-generated `__init__` annotations should preserve callable type annotations when they are introspectable. `validators.matches_re(..., func=None)` should use Python 3 full-match semantics.
expectation.conceptual: The upgrade should move consumers fully onto supported Python 3 runtimes and make attrs behave as a Python-3-native library. Users should see stable read-only metadata, native keyword-only and regex behavior, support for combining multiple iterable member validators, and more accurate typing or introspection information when converters are annotated.

constraints.grounded: Do not require or promise Python 2.7 compatibility. Keep existing public attrs contracts intact on supported Python versions: non-class inputs to `fields()` and `fields_dict()` should still raise `TypeError`, non-attrs classes should still raise `NotAnAttrsClassError`, `validators.matches_re()` should only accept `re.fullmatch`, `re.search`, `re.match`, or `None` for `func`, and `Attribute.metadata` must remain immutable from the consumer side.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must remain safe for supported Python 3 applications except where Python 2 compatibility is intentionally removed. Existing attrs validation and reflection APIs should keep their normal error behavior, and the new version should refine supported runtime semantics without changing unrelated application logic.

behavior: attrs 22.1.0 no longer supports Python 2.7 and should be consumed as a Python 3.5+ package.
When attrs builds keyword-only initializers on supported runtimes, the generated `__init__` signature uses native keyword-only parameters instead of compatibility emulation.
`validators.deep_iterable()` accepts a list or tuple of member validators and composes them so each iterable element is checked by all provided validators.
`Attribute.metadata` stores a read-only mapping proxy over a shallow copy of the original metadata mapping, so later mutations to the original mapping are not reflected in the attribute metadata.
`converters.optional()`, `converters.pipe()`, and attrs-generated `__init__` annotations retain introspectable parameter and return type annotations from annotated converters when available.
`validators.matches_re()` relies on Python 3 full-match behavior when `func` is omitted or `None`.
acceptance_criteria: When an application upgrades to attrs 22.1.0, it should target a supported Python 3 runtime and should not rely on Python 2.7 compatibility.
When `validators.deep_iterable()` is given multiple member validators as a list or tuple, each iterable element should be validated by the composed set of validators.

When attribute metadata is supplied from a mutable mapping, later changes to the original mapping should not change the exposed `Attribute.metadata`, and attempts to mutate `Attribute.metadata` should fail as for a read-only mapping.

When annotated converters are wrapped with `converters.optional()` or `converters.pipe()`, or used to derive attrs initializer annotations, the resulting callable or generated initializer should expose corresponding annotations when the converter signature is introspectable.
When `validators.matches_re()` is used without an explicit regex function, a value should pass only if the entire string matches the pattern under Python 3 full-match semantics.

task_6.title: Allow multiple member validators in deep_iterable
task_6.description: The upgrade expands `attrs.validators.deep_iterable()` so callers can supply multiple validators for each iterable element in one sequence. Those validators are treated as a combined member-validation contract while preserving existing single-validator and iterable-level validation behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `attrs.validators.deep_iterable()` supports expressing multiple per-item validation rules in a single call, so each element in the iterable can be checked against all supplied member validators without changing existing single-validator usage.

expectation.grounded: `attrs.validators.deep_iterable(member_validator, iterable_validator=None)` must accept `member_validator` as either a single callable validator or a list/tuple of callable validators. When a list or tuple is provided, it must be treated as a combined validator equivalent to wrapping the supplied validators with `attrs.validators.and_()` before applying per-item validation. Existing `iterable_validator` handling must continue to apply independently to the container itself.
expectation.conceptual: `deep_iterable()` should let callers provide multiple item-level validators together, and every element should satisfy all of them. This should behave the same as manually composing validators, while preserving the existing behavior for single validators and optional iterable-level validation.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress existing behavior when `member_validator` is already a single callable. Do not change the separate role of `iterable_validator`. Validation failures from the composed member rules must remain observable through the normal validator failure path rather than being ignored or downgraded.
constraints.conceptual: The new capability should extend, not replace, the current API. Existing uses of `deep_iterable()` should keep working, and adding multiple member validators should not weaken validation or alter container-level checks.

behavior: `deep_iterable()` now accepts a list or tuple for `member_validator` in addition to a single validator.
When multiple member validators are supplied, they are applied as one combined per-item validation contract, so each iterable element is checked against all provided validators.
If any combined member validator rejects an element, deep iterable validation fails through the standard validator error path.
If `iterable_validator` is also provided, the iterable itself continues to be validated separately from the validation applied to each element.
Existing calls that pass a single callable `member_validator` continue to behave as before.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller passes a list or tuple of valid member validators to `attrs.validators.deep_iterable()`, it should return a validator that requires every iterable element to satisfy all supplied member validators.
When any one of the supplied member validators rejects an element, validating the iterable should fail rather than accepting that element.
When `iterable_validator` is provided together with multiple member validators, the iterable itself should still be validated in addition to per-element validation.
When `member_validator` is passed as a single callable, `deep_iterable()` should preserve its previous behavior and compatibility.

task_7.title: Restore typed exports for attrs.converters and attrs.filters
task_7.description: The upgrade restores missing type-stub exposure for the public `attrs.converters` and `attrs.filters` namespaces so typed consumers can use the documented `attrs` API without missing-export issues. This is a compatibility improvement for static typing rather than a runtime feature change.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 22.1.0 exposes `attrs.converters` and `attrs.filters` correctly to typed users of the `attrs` package so those public namespaces are recognized as part of the supported API.

expectation.grounded: The `attrs` package should provide type-stub re-exports for `attrs.converters` and `attrs.filters`. Typed code and static analysis should recognize these namespaces and their public members as valid `attrs` exports, instead of treating them as missing from the package surface.
expectation.conceptual: Users who rely on type checking should be able to access the `converters` and `filters` functionality through `attrs` just like other public `attrs` namespaces, without upgrade-related missing-export problems.

constraints.grounded: This change is limited to the typed public API surface for `attrs.converters` and `attrs.filters`. It should not require new runtime semantics, and it should preserve the existing public `attrs` namespace behavior for other exports.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should improve typing compatibility only, without changing how the library behaves at runtime or disrupting existing public API usage outside the missing exports.

behavior: Static typing metadata includes `attrs.converters` as a public namespace of the `attrs` package.
Static typing metadata includes `attrs.filters` as a public namespace of the `attrs` package.
Typed consumers can reference public members under those namespaces through `attrs` without them being treated as absent from the package API.
acceptance_criteria: When a typed codebase accesses `attrs.converters`, it should be recognized as a valid public namespace of `attrs`.
When a typed codebase accesses `attrs.filters`, it should be recognized as a valid public namespace of `attrs`.
When static analysis inspects code that uses public members from `attrs.converters` or `attrs.filters`, it should not report those namespaces as missing from `attrs`.
When upgrading from 21.4.0 to 22.1.0, this change should not introduce any new runtime-only behavior requirements for users who already rely on the existing `attrs` API.

task_8.title: Add missing type stubs for cmp_using
task_8.description: The upgrade adds missing typing support for the existing `cmp_using()` API exposed by `attr` and `attrs`. This improves static type checking and editor/tooling recognition of the comparator helper without changing runtime behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 22.1.0 exposes `cmp_using()` as a supported public API in typing-aware usage so developers can reference `attr.cmp_using()` and `attrs.cmp_using()` without static-analysis errors.

expectation.grounded: The published type information for the library should declare `cmp_using()` on both the `attr` and `attrs` public namespaces. Static type checkers and IDEs should recognize the API as present and callable in the same way as the runtime package already exposes it.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, the library should fully advertise its comparator-construction helper to typing tools, so typed projects can use the existing API without false missing-attribute or missing-symbol reports.

constraints.grounded: This is a stub-surface update only: it should not alter the runtime availability, runtime semantics, or import behavior of existing public APIs beyond making `cmp_using()` visible to typing consumers.
constraints.conceptual: The change should improve developer tooling support only, while preserving existing runtime behavior and avoiding unrelated API changes.

behavior: Typed access to `attr.cmp_using` is recognized as part of the public API.
Typed access to `attrs.cmp_using` is recognized as part of the public API.
Static analysis no longer treats `cmp_using()` as missing from the library's top-level public namespaces.
The upgrade affects typing and editor support rather than runtime execution behavior.
acceptance_criteria: When a typed project references `attr.cmp_using()`, it should be recognized as a valid public API by static analysis tools.
When a typed project references `attrs.cmp_using()`, it should be recognized as a valid public API by static analysis tools.
When users upgrade from 21.4.0 to 22.1.0, the change should remove false typing/tooling complaints about `cmp_using()` being absent.
The upgrade should not introduce a user-visible runtime behavior change for existing `cmp_using()` usage.

task_9.title: Complete attrs in_() validation error payload
task_9.description: The upgrade corrects the runtime error contract of `attrs.validators.in_()` so failed membership validation raises a complete `ValueError` payload instead of only a human-readable message. This aligns the validator with its documented behavior and makes failure handling more consistent with other attrs validators.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that failed `attrs.validators.in_()` membership validation exposes a complete, structured `ValueError` payload so applications can reliably inspect the invalid attribute, the allowed options, and the rejected value when handling validation failures.

expectation.grounded: When `attrs.validators.in_(options)` rejects a value, it should raise `ValueError` whose arguments include the human-readable validation message together with the attribute object, the validator's `options`, and the invalid value. This should apply consistently for supported option containers such as sequences and strings, matching the documented public behavior of `in_()`.
expectation.conceptual: Membership validation failures from `in_()` should provide both a readable error and structured context about what failed, so callers can present, log, or transform the error without guessing from text alone.

constraints.grounded: The upgrade must preserve the existing validation trigger and continue raising `ValueError` on rejected values; it should extend the exception payload rather than changing the validator's purpose or replacing the human-readable error. Successful validations and unrelated validators must remain unaffected.
constraints.conceptual: The change should only enrich failure details for the same invalid inputs, without altering normal successful behavior or changing which situations count as membership validation failures.

behavior: A failed `attrs.validators.in_()` check still raises `ValueError` at runtime when the value is not contained in the configured options.
The raised `ValueError` now carries structured context beyond the text message: the validated attribute, the configured options, and the rejected value are included in the exception arguments.
The human-readable validation message remains part of the `ValueError`, but it is no longer the only error argument.
The structured failure payload is available for different option types accepted by `in_()`, including iterable collections and strings.
acceptance_criteria: When `attrs.validators.in_(options)` validates a value that is not a member of `options`, it should raise `ValueError` containing both a readable validation message and structured failure context.
When handling that `ValueError`, application code should be able to retrieve the attribute being validated, the configured allowed options, and the invalid value from the exception arguments.
When the invalid membership check is performed against string options or collection options, the same complete `ValueError` shape should be exposed.
When the value is a member of the configured options, `attrs.validators.in_()` should continue to succeed without raising.

task_10.title: Add official Python 3.11 support in attrs 22.1.0
task_10.description: Upgrade to attrs 22.1.0 so applications can run on Python 3.11 as an officially supported interpreter. The runtime compatibility change centers on how the library updates closure cells on modern Python versions, avoiding interpreter-specific failures while preserving older-version behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading from attrs 21.4.0 to 22.1.0 officially supports Python 3.11 and that runtime features depending on internal closure-cell updates continue to work correctly on supported Python versions.

expectation.grounded: The attrs package should declare Python 3.11 as a supported runtime. On Python 3.8 and newer, the closure-cell update path used by attr._compat.make_set_closure_cell must work on Python 3.11 without relying on code-object rewriting assumptions that are incompatible with newer interpreters. On Python versions below 3.8, the pre-existing fallback behavior should remain available.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to adopt attrs 22.1.0 on Python 3.11 with the expectation that the library is officially supported there and that runtime-generated attrs behavior continues to function normally across supported Python versions.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress compatibility for supported pre-3.8 runtimes that still require the legacy closure-cell mutation path. The upgrade should change runtime compatibility behavior only where needed for Python 3.11 support and should not alter the public contract beyond adding Python 3.11 support.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should expand interpreter compatibility without breaking existing supported environments or changing normal attrs behavior for users outside the new Python 3.11 support boundary.

behavior: Package metadata recognizes Python 3.11 as a supported interpreter.
On Python 3.8 and newer, closure-cell updates used internally by attrs succeed through the interpreter-compatible modern path, including on Python 3.11.
On older supported Python versions, attrs retains the legacy closure-cell update path instead of forcing the modern behavior everywhere.
acceptance_criteria: When attrs 22.1.0 is evaluated for supported runtimes, Python 3.11 should be included as an officially supported Python version.
When attrs performs runtime behavior that depends on updating a closure cell on Python 3.11, it should complete successfully without failing because of incompatible code-object assumptions.
When the same closure-cell update logic runs on Python 3.8 through Python 3.10, it should continue to work through the modern compatibility path.
When attrs runs on older supported Python versions that need the legacy compatibility path, existing behavior should remain intact.
